newsitem.title: CANADA: ATHLETICS-BEN JOHNSON WITHDRAWS IAAF REINSTATEMENT BID.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-BEN JOHNSON WITHDRAWS IAAF REINSTATEMENT BID.

text.p: Disgraced Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson on Tuesday withdrew his bid before the IAAF to lift a lifetime ban while he awaits his day in a Canadian court.

Johnson filed suit in an Ontario court earlier this month to win the right to race again and prove he is still the world's fastest man. But the court said Tuesday it will not hear the case until July 21, postponing any comeback for Johnson for at least another two months.

"There is disappointment, but...I have to be patient and hopefully everything will work in my favour," said the now 35-year-old Johnson, still trying to recover from the sport's most infamous doping case in 1988.

Johnson won the 100 meters gold medal at the Seoul Olympics, clocking a record 9.79 seconds. But he was stripped of his medal and his world record stricken from the books after he tested positive for anabolic steroids in Seoul.
Johnson was banned from competition for two years, and at an official Canadian inquiry into drugs in sport that followed the scandal, he admitted to many years of illegal steroid use.

In 1993, Johnson was banned for life after a test found high levels of testosterone in his system. He has denied using an illegal substance and his lawyers argued that the IAAF, which rules international athletics, did not give their client a fair hearing.
The suit alleges that Johnson's ban violated his ability to earn a living.
Johnson's lawyers had hoped a favourable court ruling Tuesday would pressure the IAAF into overturning the ban at its two-day meeting in Athens starting Thursday.
But lawyers for Athletics Canada and the IAAF won an adjournment until July 21, prompting Johnson's people to drop their application before the IAAF.
"We withdraw because it is best that our judge rule on it rather than letting the IAAF," said Johnson's agent Morris Chrobotek. "Restraint of trade is a Canadian case."

Johnson's lawyers said they were encouraged by past IAAF statements that it was willing to follow the rule of local jurisdictions. They hope the ban will be lifted if the Canadian court agrees that Johnson's right to earn a living had been violated.
Johnson has tried his hand at other sports since 1993, such as professional football and soccer, but met with little success. And the money he earned as one of the world's elite runners is dwindling.
"He's got a little bit left to keep him going, but he has to get back to work," Chrobotek said.
Meanwhile, Johnson said he was training five hours a day, six days a week as he anxiously awaits a ruling that he hopes will give him a chance for a comeback.
"I just need one or two races to sharpen up and I'm ready," he said.
